claims.text: Sliding wear stress drives localized elemental segregation at the HEA wear interface.
Localized elemental segregation triggers in situ formation of protective oxides or transformation-induced hard phases.
The in situ protective phase governs the improved wear resistance of HEA coatings.
The initial coating is nominally homogeneous and has not been pre-conditioned to alter segregation tendencies.
A targeted heat treatment can modify the coating's tendency to redistribute elements locally under wear stress.
The targeted heat treatment increases the predisposition for elemental segregation during wear.
Mechanically stressed segregated regions transform into a protective phase.
The protective phase acts as a barrier to further material removal.
Protective oxide-layer formation can increase HEA wear resistance during elevated-temperature reciprocating wear in atmospheric conditions.
Heat-treated coatings will have systematically lower wear volume than untreated coatings.
Heat-treated coatings may have a lower coefficient of friction than untreated coatings.
Increasing wear-test temperature can slightly decrease the coefficient of friction in an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA.
The proposed effect should hold across typical application wear stresses and from room to moderately elevated temperatures.
The stress and temperature thresholds for the effect depend on the specific HEA composition.
Identically tested heat-treated and untreated coatings provide a controlled comparison of the proposed intervention.
Wear volume, coefficient of friction, microscopy, elemental mapping, and phase analysis can test the predicted outcome and proposed mediator.
The hypothesis is falsified if heat treatment yields neither a statistically significant wear or friction improvement nor evidence of segregation-induced protective-phase formation.
